title: Prehistoric South Arabia
subtitle: 8,000–1,200 BC · The Highland Neolithic, the Cattle Cult and the Roots of the Incense Kingdoms

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: No king-lists, no inscriptions — the record runs from the first Holocene herders, through the cattle-cult horizon, to the Bronze Age villages of the highlands and the great coastal town of Sabir

entries.group: Neolithic Foragers and First Herders (8000–4000 BC)
entries.label: Holocene herders enter the southern highlands
entries.loc: the Dhamar highlands and the Hadramawt wadis, Yemen
entries.hint: As the early Holocene monsoon pushed rain deep into the south, foraging groups and the first cattle-, sheep- and goat-herders spread across the Yemen highlands and the perennial wadis of the Hadramawt. This is the population whose descendants would build the cattle monuments and, three thousand years later, the terraced villages.
entries.note: the RASA (Roots of Agriculture in Southern Arabia / AHSD) project, McCorriston and Harrower; the Dhamar Survey Project, Wilkinson, Edens and Gibson, 'Sabaean irrigated agriculture... the central highlands of Yemen', Antiquity / AAE (1999).

entries.group: Neolithic Foragers and First Herders (8000–4000 BC)
entries.label: Manayzah rockshelter, Wadi Sana
entries.loc: Wadi Sana, Hadramawt plateau, Yemen
entries.hint: The stratified deposits at Manayzah hold the earliest securely dated domestic cattle, sheep and goat in southern Arabia, alongside the fine pressure-flaked points of the Arabian bifacial tradition. It is the anchor site for the region's Neolithic chronology.
entries.note: McCorriston, Harrower et al., RASA project excavation reports; Crassard on the Manayzah lithic sequence, 'Wadi Sana and the Neolithic of Hadramawt', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy.

entries.label: The turret tombs of the Hadramawt plateau
entries.loc: the jol plateau above Wadi Sana and Wadi Idim, Yemen
entries.hint: Thousands of drystone 'High Circular Tombs' line the ridgelines of the Hadramawt plateau, built and reused over two millennia by mobile pastoralists. Placed to be seen from the valleys below, they map a segmentary society onto the landscape without a single settlement or ruler's name.
entries.note: RASA project tomb surveys; earlier recording by the Soviet-Yemeni Complex Expedition (Sedov, Griaznevich). Harrower and McCorriston, 'Ancient territories... the Hadramawt', in the RASA synthesis volumes.

entries.label: The Kheshiya cattle-skull monument
entries.loc: Wadi Sana, Hadramawt, Yemen
entries.hint: On a low rise in Wadi Sana, herders laid out a ring of some forty cattle crania in a single act, brought from many different herds and buried together. It is the oldest monumental construction known in South Arabia and the clearest sign of supra-household cooperation before the historic kingdoms.
entries.note: McCorriston, Harrower, Martin et al., 'Cattle cults of the Arabian Neolithic and early territorial societies', American Anthropologist 114 (2012).

entries.group: The Bronze Age: The Highlands (2500–1200 BC)
entries.label: The Bronze Age culture of Khawlan at-Tiyal
entries.loc: Wadi Yanaʿim and al-Masannah, east of Sanaa, Yemen
entries.hint: The Italian Archaeological Mission found a network of small drystone villages in the highlands east of Sanaa — permanent houses, terraced fields, storage and a settled domestic assemblage. This 'Khawlan Bronze Age' is the first evidence of village life in the Yemeni highlands and the immediate ancestor of the Sabaean settlement pattern.
entries.note: Alessandro de Maigret (ed.), 'The Bronze Age Culture of Hawlan at-Tiyal and al-Hada (Republic of Yemen)', IsMEO, Rome (1990).

entries.group: The Bronze Age: The Highlands (2500–1200 BC)
entries.label: The Dhamar plain villages
entries.loc: the Dhamar–Yarim plateau, Yemen
entries.hint: Survey and excavation on the Dhamar plain traced dozens of small Bronze Age farming settlements exploiting runoff from the surrounding slopes. Their check-dams and field walls are the technological seed of the hydraulic agriculture the Sabaeans later scaled to the Marib Dam.
entries.note: the Dhamar Survey Project — T. J. Wilkinson, C. Edens, McGuire Gibson; Wilkinson and Edens, 'Survey and excavation in the central highlands of Yemen', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 10 (1999).

entries.group: The Bronze Age: The Tihama Coast (2400–1200 BC)
entries.label: Al-Midamman, a Bronze Age centre on the Tihama
entries.loc: the mouth of Wadi Rimaʿ, Tihama coast, Yemen
entries.hint: Near the Red Sea shore, al-Midamman combined a field of standing stones, a bronze workshop casting axes and daggers on site, and an industry making granite grinding-stones for trade along the coast. It is the type-site for the Tihama's own Bronze Age, distinct from the highland villages.
entries.note: Edward J. Keall, Royal Ontario Museum Tihama Coastal Survey; Keall, 'Possibilities for a maritime cultural landscape... al-Midamman', and annual reports in the Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies (1998–2005).

entries.group: The Bronze Age: Sabir and the Aden Coast (1900–1200 BC)
entries.label: Sabir (Maʿlayba), the great Tihama town
entries.loc: Maʿlayba, near Lahij and Aden, Yemen
entries.hint: Spread over roughly a square kilometre of mudbrick housing behind the Aden coast, Sabir supported thousands of people on sorghum agriculture, fishing and trade across the mouth of the Red Sea. Its distinctive pottery defines the 'Sabir culture', the largest second-millennium settlement known anywhere in Arabia.
entries.note: Burkhard Vogt and Alexander Sedov, 'The Sabir culture and coastal Yemen during the second millennium BC', Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt, subsequent Maʿlayba reports.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: There is almost no direct evidence of organised violence — only tomb-covered ridgelines that look like territorial signalling, a coast full of cached weapons, and the quiet emptying of the largest town

entries.label: The tomb ridgelines as a landscape of competition
entries.loc: the Hadramawt plateau, Yemen
entries.hint: The turret tombs cluster on the skylines between grazing territories, not at random. Their excavators read them as a segmentary pastoral society marking and defending access to scarce water and pasture through monument-building rather than through any recorded warfare.
entries.note: McCorriston, 'Pilgrimage and Household in the Ancient Near East' (2011); RASA territorial-signalling models. No named battle or enemy survives — the inference is from tomb placement.

entries.label: The bronze weapon hoards of al-Midamman
entries.loc: al-Midamman, Tihama coast, Yemen
entries.hint: Al-Midamman produced groups of cast bronze axes, daggers and spearheads deposited together. Whether they are votive offerings, a smith's stock, or caches hidden against raiding is unresolved — but they are the densest concentration of Bronze Age weaponry in South Arabia.
entries.note: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey reports; Giumlia-Mair et al., metallurgical study of the al-Midamman bronzes, in Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies (2002).

entries.label: Sabir contracts and is abandoned
entries.loc: Maʿlayba, near Aden, Yemen
entries.hint: By the end of the second millennium the largest town in Arabia had emptied. The excavators cannot yet fix the cause — a weakening monsoon, a shifting coastline cutting off its harbour, or competition from the rising highland polities — but Sabir's fall sits exactly at the threshold of the literate Sabaean period.
entries.note: Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt on the Maʿlayba sequence. The handoff to the emerging kingdom of Sabaʾ is this folio's framing.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Collective ritual, boundary tombs and the first floodwater channels are the visible infrastructure of social organisation — there are no palaces until the very end

entries.label: Cattle-skull deposition as a corporate act
entries.loc: Wadi Sana, Hadramawt, Yemen
entries.hint: The forty-odd animals in the Kheshiya ring came from many separate herds, meaning dispersed households pooled livestock and labour for one event. It is the earliest archaeological evidence in South Arabia of decision-making above the level of a single family — an incipient territorial society.
entries.note: McCorriston et al., American Anthropologist 114 (2012); the corporate-cooperation reading is the excavators' own.

entries.label: The turret tombs as boundary infrastructure
entries.loc: the jol plateau, Hadramawt, Yemen
entries.hint: Chains of tombs along the plateau edges delimit the grazing territories of pastoral clans, tying lineage identity to a specific stretch of land. They function as property markers and social memory at once, maintained across dozens of generations.
entries.note: Harrower and McCorriston, RASA synthesis; comparison drawn by the project to the funerary-avenue landscape of northwest Arabia.

entries.label: The first floodwater irrigation in the highland wadis
entries.loc: the Dhamar plain and Wadi Yanaʿim, Yemen
entries.hint: Bronze Age villages in the highlands built low stone barriers to slow wadi floods and spread the silt-laden water across fields. Small and local, this runoff farming is the technique — and the organisational habit — that the kingdom of Sabaʾ would later scale up into the monumental irrigation works of Marib.
entries.note: Michael Harrower, 'Water Histories and Spatial Archaeology: Ancient Yemen and the American West' (2016); Dhamar Survey Project, Wilkinson and Edens (1999).

entries.label: Sabir's monumental architecture and zoned quarters
entries.loc: Maʿlayba, near Aden, Yemen
entries.hint: At its centre Sabir had a large mudbrick platform building set apart from the ordinary housing, with the settlement laid out in distinguishable zones around it. This is the earliest public architecture and planned settlement known in South Arabia, four centuries before the first royal inscriptions.
entries.note: Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt, 'The Sabir Culture and the coastal plain of the Republic of Yemen', later Maʿlayba reports.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A herder religion built on cattle and the ancestors, and an aniconic standing-stone cult on the coast — both early phases of traditions that run through pre-Islamic Arabia for millennia

entries.label: The South Arabian cattle cult
entries.loc: Wadi Sana and the southern highlands, Yemen
entries.hint: The Kheshiya skull ring, cattle bucrania in tombs, and long-horned cattle dominating the rock art together describe a religion centred on the herd — an appeal for fertility and rain expressed through the sacrifice and display of the animals a pastoral society depended on.
entries.note: McCorriston et al., American Anthropologist 114 (2012); parallels with the cattle burials of the northeast-Arabian Neolithic and the Saharan cattle cult are drawn explicitly in the RASA literature.

entries.label: The standing stones of al-Midamman
entries.loc: al-Midamman, Tihama coast, Yemen
entries.hint: Rows of undressed monoliths, some over three metres tall, were raised in a deliberate field near the shore. This aniconic standing-stone cult — worship focused on an unworked stone rather than an image — is the South Arabian branch of the betyl tradition that recurs across pre-Islamic Arabia down to the Nabataeans.
entries.note: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey, PSAS reports (1998–2005); the long continuity of Arabian betyl worship is a standard observation in Nabataean religious studies (Healey, 'The Religion of the Nabataeans', 2001).

entries.label: The ancestors on the skyline
entries.loc: the Hadramawt plateau, Yemen
entries.hint: Burying the dead in visible ridge-top tombs kept the ancestors permanently in view of the living and bound each lineage to its territory. Tombs were reopened and reused over centuries, making them the fixed points of a mobile society's identity.
entries.note: RASA project mortuary studies; Soviet-Yemeni Complex Expedition tomb recording (Griaznevich, Sedov).

entries.label: Dolmen and cist burial in the highlands
entries.loc: Khawlan at-Tiyal, east of Sanaa, Yemen
entries.hint: The Bronze Age villagers of Khawlan buried their dead in stone-slab cists and small dolmens grouped into cemeteries, furnished with pottery, beads and occasional bronze. The shift from the plateau's collective turret tombs to family graves tracks the shift from mobile herding to settled village life.
entries.note: de Maigret (ed.), 'The Bronze Age Culture of Hawlan at-Tiyal' (1990).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: A long rock-art tradition of cattle, hunters and dancers; a distinctive coastal pottery; monumental stone-raising; and fine bronze and bead craft

entries.label: The rock art of the Yemen highlands
entries.loc: the highlands around Sanaa, Saʿda and Najran
entries.hint: Thousands of engraved and pecked panels across the highlands show long-horned cattle, ostriches, ibex, hunters with bows, and files of human figures. The tradition runs from the Neolithic cattle-keepers into the Bronze Age, a continuous visual record of a society that left no texts.
entries.note: Madeleine Garcia and Mounir Arbach / A. Rachad, 'À la découverte des oasis oubliées du Yémen' and the CEFAS rock-art surveys; Anati and Jung on Yemeni highland rock art.

entries.label: Sabir Ware
entries.loc: the Aden coast and southern Tihama, Yemen
entries.hint: Hand-made, dark-burnished pottery with incised geometric bands and applied knobs is the signature of the Sabir culture — consistent enough across the southern coast to be the marker archaeologists use to trace the culture's reach.
entries.note: Buffa and Vogt, ceramic analysis in the Maʿlayba reports; Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998).

entries.label: The al-Midamman megalith field
entries.loc: al-Midamman, Tihama coast, Yemen
entries.hint: Raising a field of multi-tonne granite monoliths on the flat coastal plain was a feat of organised communal labour visible for kilometres — the Tihama's answer to the monumental architecture that the highlands expressed through terraces and villages.
entries.note: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey, PSAS (1998–2005).

entries.label: Cast bronze axes, daggers and pins
entries.loc: al-Midamman and Khawlan at-Tiyal, Yemen
entries.hint: The bronzeworkers of al-Midamman and the highland villages produced shaft-hole axes, riveted daggers and long decorated pins, some with deliberate surface patination. Metallurgical analysis shows a controlled use of arsenic and tin, not accidental alloying.
entries.note: Giumlia-Mair, Keall et al., metallurgical study of al-Midamman bronzes, PSAS (2002); de Maigret (1990) on the Khawlan metal assemblage.

entries.label: Shell, carnelian and stone ornament
entries.loc: across the Tihama, the highlands and the Hadramawt
entries.hint: Red Sea shell pendants, ground stone beads and imported carnelian appear in graves from the Neolithic onward — the one category of personal display that survives across the whole span, and evidence of exchange reaching the Indus bead world by the Bronze Age.
entries.note: grave assemblages published in de Maigret (1990), Vogt and Sedov (1998), and the RASA mortuary reports; carnelian sourcing discussed in Boivin and Fuller (2009).

entries.label: Dancers and rattles in the highland rock art
entries.loc: the highlands around Sanaa and Saʿda, Yemen
entries.hint: Panels of linked human figures with raised arms, some holding curved objects read as rattles or throwing-sticks, are interpreted as depictions of dance and communal ceremony — the only trace of music and performance from preliterate South Arabia.
entries.note: Garcia and Rachad, CEFAS rock-art surveys; the dance interpretation follows Jung and Anati's readings of the highland corpus. Flagged as interpretive — no instruments survive from this period.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Flotation samples, GIS survey models and radiocarbon dates are how this era is known — there is no written word from it

entries.label: Archaeobotany rewrites South Arabia's agricultural origins
entries.loc: Sabir, Wadi Sana and the Dhamar plain, Yemen
entries.hint: Systematic sieving and flotation at Sabir and the RASA sites recovered charred sorghum, wheat, barley and pulses, turning the question of when — and from where — farming reached South Arabia into an evidence-based debate rather than a guess from later texts.
entries.note: Nicole Boivin and Dorian Fuller, 'Shell middens, ships and seeds: exploring coastal subsistence, maritime trade and the dispersal of domesticates in and around the ancient Arabian Peninsula', Journal of World Prehistory 22 (2009); RASA archaeobotanical reports.

entries.label: Landscape survey reconstructs a society with no texts
entries.loc: the central highlands, Yemen
entries.hint: The Dhamar Survey Project and the RASA project used systematic field-walking, aerial imagery and GIS modelling to reconstruct settlement, land use and territory for a period that left no king-lists — demonstrating that a preliterate society can be written about in detail from its landscape alone.
entries.note: Wilkinson, Edens and Gibson, Dhamar Survey Project publications (Antiquity 1997, AAE 1999); Harrower, 'Water Histories and Spatial Archaeology' (2016).

entries.label: Building an absolute chronology for the Bronze Age
entries.loc: Khawlan at-Tiyal and Maʿlayba, Yemen
entries.hint: With no inscriptions to date the second millennium BC in Yemen, radiocarbon series from de Maigret's Khawlan villages and Vogt's Sabir soundings established the framework everyone still uses: a highland Bronze Age from c.2500 BC and a coastal one running to c.1200 BC.
entries.note: de Maigret (ed.) (1990); Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A herding interior, terraced highland farms, sorghum on the coast, obsidian and shell on the Red Sea — and the first thin traces of the aromatics trade

entries.label: Cattle, sheep and goat pastoralism
entries.loc: the highlands and the Hadramawt, Yemen
entries.hint: Mobile herding was the economic base of the interior for six thousand years. Isotope work on animal teeth and the seasonality of the plateau sites show herds moved between the highland pastures in summer and the sheltered wadis in winter.
entries.note: RASA zooarchaeology; McCorriston et al. (2012).

entries.label: Highland terrace agriculture begins
entries.loc: Khawlan at-Tiyal and the Dhamar plain, Yemen
entries.hint: The Bronze Age villages of the highlands farmed terraced plots of wheat, barley, grapes and pulses cut into the slopes — the earliest phase of the terraced agriculture that still shapes highland Yemen, and the surplus that made permanent villages possible.
entries.note: de Maigret (ed.) (1990); Wilkinson and Edens, AAE 10 (1999).

entries.label: Sorghum and the summer-crop economy of the Tihama
entries.loc: Maʿlayba and the southern Tihama, Yemen
entries.hint: Sabir grew sorghum — an African summer cereal watered by the monsoon rains that fall on the coastal plain — which let a much denser population settle the Tihama than dryland herding ever could. It is the earliest sorghum cultivation known in Arabia.
entries.note: Boivin and Fuller (2009); Sabir archaeobotanical reports (Vogt, Buffa).

entries.label: Obsidian exchange across the southern Red Sea
entries.loc: the Yemen highlands and the Tihama coast
entries.hint: Volcanic glass from the Yemeni highlands and from Ethiopian sources moved in both directions across the strait of Bab al-Mandab, traced to its origin by geochemical fingerprinting in Neolithic contexts. It is the earliest documented long-distance trade in the region.
entries.note: Lamya Khalidi, 'Holocene obsidian exchange in the Red Sea region', in 'The Evolution of Human Populations in Arabia' (2010); Zarins on Tihama obsidian.

entries.label: Marine foraging and the Tihama shell middens
entries.loc: the Red Sea littoral of the Tihama, Yemen
entries.hint: Mounds of discarded shell along the coast record populations living on fish, shellfish and dugong long before and alongside farming. The Red Sea shore was a productive niche in its own right, not a marginal one.
entries.note: Khalidi, Tihama coastal survey; Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey; Bökönyi faunal analyses.

entries.label: The first traces of the aromatics economy
entries.loc: the Hadramawt, Dhofar borderland and southern highlands
entries.hint: Frankincense and myrrh trees grow wild in the Hadramawt and the Dhofar hills. Direct evidence for their collection and trade before the first millennium BC is still thin, but Egyptian demand for South Arabian and African incense in the Bronze Age implies the network was already turning.
entries.note: Nigel Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh: A Study of the Arabian Incense Trade' (1981); the pre-first-millennium evidence is reviewed and treated cautiously by Singer (2007). Flagged: indirect.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Pressure-flaked stone tools kept in use for millennia, on-site bronze casting on the coast, and the runoff-irrigation technique that would build the Marib Dam

entries.label: The Arabian bifacial lithic tradition
entries.loc: Wadi Sana and across South Arabia
entries.hint: The South Arabian Neolithic toolkit — barbed and tanged arrowheads, bifacial knives and borers, worked by fine pressure-flaking — stayed in use for thousands of years after metal appeared in the Near East, a self-sufficient technology suited to a mobile pastoral life.
entries.note: Crassard on the Manayzah and Wadi Sana lithics; Charpentier on the Arabian bifacial tradition, in 'The Evolution of Human Populations in Arabia' (2010).

entries.label: On-site bronze casting at al-Midamman
entries.loc: al-Midamman, Tihama coast, Yemen
entries.hint: Crucible fragments, moulds and casting waste show axes and daggers were made at al-Midamman itself, using deliberate arsenical and tin bronze. It is among the earliest metal-production sites in South Arabia and the only well-documented Bronze Age workshop on the Red Sea coast of Arabia.
entries.note: Giumlia-Mair, Keall et al., PSAS (2002); Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey reports.

entries.label: Check-dams and runoff field systems
entries.loc: the Dhamar plain and the highland wadis, Yemen
entries.hint: Low stone barriers thrown across wadi beds slowed the seasonal floods and let their silt settle on the fields — a small-scale technique for turning erratic rain into a crop. Sabaʾ would inherit it and scale it up into the sluices and embankments of the Great Dam of Marib.
entries.note: Harrower, 'Water Histories and Spatial Archaeology' (2016); on the later Marib scale-up, Brunner and the DAI Marib Dam studies.

entries.label: The granite grinding-stone industry
entries.loc: al-Midamman, Tihama coast, Yemen
entries.hint: Al-Midamman quarried and shaped granite querns and hand-grinders in quantity, well beyond local need, and traded them along the Tihama. Specialised production for exchange is itself a marker of an economy past pure subsistence.
entries.note: Keall, ROM Tihama Coastal Survey, PSAS (1998–2005).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The mouth of the Red Sea as a two-way channel — obsidian, pottery styles and African crops crossing it — and the far edge of Egypt's search for incense

entries.label: Obsidian across the Bab al-Mandab
entries.loc: the strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa
entries.hint: The oldest long-distance exchange in the region ran across the twenty-mile strait: highland-Yemeni obsidian reached the African coast and Ethiopian obsidian reached the Tihama and the highlands, a maritime connection older than farming on either shore.
entries.note: Khalidi, 'Holocene obsidian exchange in the Red Sea region' (2010).

entries.label: The Tihama–Horn of Africa interaction sphere
entries.loc: the southern Red Sea coasts, Yemen, Eritrea and Sudan
entries.hint: Sabir and al-Midamman pottery shares vessel forms and decoration with the Gash Group of the Sudanese–Eritrean lowlands and with sites near the Gulf of Tadjoura. The Bronze Age Red Sea was a single cultural sphere straddling both shores, not a boundary.
entries.note: Andrea Manzo, 'Italian archaeological expedition to the Sudan... the Gash Delta'; Fattovich on Red Sea cultural interaction; Keall on Tihama–African ceramic links.

entries.label: African crops move into Arabia
entries.loc: the Tihama coast, Yemen
entries.hint: Sorghum — and in the following centuries finger millet and cowpea — crossed from Africa into the Arabian summer-rainfall zone, part of a two-way biological exchange across the Red Sea that also moved Near Eastern wheat and barley south.
entries.note: Boivin and Fuller, Journal of World Prehistory 22 (2009).

entries.label: Egypt, Punt and the Red Sea incense trade
entries.loc: Deir el-Bahari, Egypt (the Punt reliefs) — and the southern Red Sea
entries.hint: Egyptian seaborne expeditions to the 'God's Land' of Punt for incense, myrrh, gold and ebony are recorded from Sahure to Hatshepsut's famous voyage of about 1470 BC. Whether Punt reached across to the South Arabian coast or lay only on the African side is still argued, but the aromatics network it tapped was already Bronze Age.
entries.note: the Punt reliefs in Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari; the location debate — Kitchen for both shores, Meeks and others for Africa only.

entries.label: The thin link toward the Gulf and Mesopotamia
entries.loc: the eastern Hadramawt and the interior sands
entries.hint: A handful of shared bead types and imports hint that Bronze Age South Arabia was not entirely sealed off from the Magan and Dilmun worlds of the northeast. The evidence is slight — but it is not absent, and future work along the interior route may thicken it.
entries.note: synthesis; de Maigret (1990) on imports in the Khawlan assemblage. Flagged: currently thin.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A monsoon that greened the south and then withdrew, forcing populations onto the highlands and the springs — and, at the end, the coalescence of the caravan kingdoms

entries.label: The Holocene Humid Period in the south
entries.loc: the Yemen highlands and the Ramlat as-Sabatayn margins
entries.hint: A stronger Indian Ocean monsoon filled highland lakes, ran the wadis year-round and pushed vegetation deep into what is now desert. This wet window is the environmental setting for the whole South Arabian Neolithic.
entries.note: Anne-Marie Lézine, palaeolake and pollen records from Yemen; the Qunf and Hoti cave speleothem records from neighbouring Oman (Fleitmann et al.) anchor the regional monsoon history.

entries.label: Aridification and the retreat to the highlands
entries.loc: across South Arabia
entries.hint: As the monsoon weakened, people concentrated where water persisted — the highland catchments, the perennial wadis of the Hadramawt, the springs of the Tihama. The distribution of historic Yemen's population was set by this contraction.
entries.note: Lézine, Yemeni palaeoenvironmental syntheses; Parker and Rose on the wider Arabian mid-Holocene aridification.

entries.label: The two South Arabias diverge
entries.loc: the highlands and the southern coast, Yemen
entries.hint: By the late Bronze Age the terraced-village highland world of Khawlan and the sorghum-farming coastal world of Sabir were distinct societies — different crops, different architecture, different pottery. The split between highland and Tihama Yemen persists into the present.
entries.note: synthesis of Vogt and Sedov (1998) and de Maigret (1990).

entries.label: The thread continues — Sabaʾ and the caravan kingdoms
entries.loc: Marib and the Ramlat as-Sabatayn oases, Yemen
entries.hint: This folio stops at 1200 BC because the evidence thins here, not because the history does. Within a few centuries the highland irrigation communities coalesce around the oasis of Marib into the kingdom of Sabaʾ, monumental dam-building begins, and Ancient South Arabian writing appears.
entries.note: a forward reference: the successor folio south-arabia-1200bc-300bc (the early Sabaean and Minaean period) is planned but not yet built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A mostly invisible herding majority, the thousands of townspeople of Sabir, and the daily grind of turning grain into food

entries.label: The mobile pastoral majority
entries.loc: the highlands and the Hadramawt, Yemen
entries.hint: For most of this span most South Arabians were herders who built no permanent houses. They survive as tomb clusters, hearth scatters and stone-tool debris across the plateau — a population visible as a landscape pattern rather than as families or names.
entries.note: RASA project; the same caution the project applies against reading a mobile society as an empty one.

entries.label: The people of Sabir
entries.loc: Maʿlayba, near Aden, Yemen
entries.hint: Several thousand people lived at Sabir farming sorghum, fishing the coast and trading across the strait, drawing on both Arabian and African connections. They are the nearest thing this folio has to a named, describable community — and their town was abandoned within living memory of the first Sabaean inscriptions.
entries.note: Vogt and Sedov, PSAS 28 (1998); Buffa and Vogt, Maʿlayba reports.

entries.label: Grinding grain: household labour in the Bronze Age
entries.loc: Khawlan, al-Midamman and Sabir, Yemen
entries.hint: Querns and hand-grinders are among the commonest finds at every Bronze Age settlement in South Arabia. Behind each one lies hours of daily food-processing labour, in most traditional societies women's work — the unglamorous economic foundation under every village and town in this folio.
entries.note: household archaeology of the Khawlan villages (de Maigret 1990) and Sabir (Vogt and Sedov 1998); Keall on the scale of the al-Midamman grinding-stone industry.
